title: Search a 2D Matrix
summary: You get a grid `matrix` of integers with m rows and n columns, and an integer `target`. The numbers in each row are sorted from smallest to largest, and each row starts with a number larger than the last number of the row above it. Return true if `target` is somewhere in the grid and false if it isn't. The search must take O(log(m·n)) time.

examples.explanation: 18 is the third number in the middle row.
5 would come between 3 and 8, where the first row ends and the second begins, but it isn't in the grid.

approaches.twist: Treat the rows as one sorted list of m·n numbers, and turn each middle index into a row and a column with divmod.
Binary search the first column to find the one row that could hold the target, then binary search inside that row.
Check every cell, row by row, and return true as soon as one equals the target.
approaches.note: Works, but it may read all m·n cells: O(m·n) time. The target is O(log(m·n)).

signals.meaning: In sorted order, the middle number tells you which side the target must be on, so one check rules out half of what's left.

signals.phrase: larger than the last number of the row above
signals.meaning: The rows chain into one sorted list of m·n numbers. Position i in that list is row i // n and column i % n, and divmod(i, n) gives both at once.
Reading every cell is O(m·n). To reach log(m·n), each check has to halve all the cells still in play, not just one row.
The input is a 2D grid, though a little index math lets you search it as if it were one flat list.

constraintReading: The grid holds at most 100·100 = 10⁴ numbers, so even reading every cell would be quick: the O(log(m·n)) requirement is what rules out O(m·n). Counting all m·n cells as the input size, that target is the Plan card's O(log n), at most 14 halvings for 10⁴ cells. Binary searching each row, O(m log n), or walking in from a corner, O(m + n), also falls short.

hints.clarify: How do the rows fit together? Each row is sorted, and each row starts above where the previous one ended, so reading the rows one after another gives one sorted list. Try [[1, 4], [6, 9]] by hand: read row by row it's [1, 4, 6, 9], and 6 is at position 2 of that list, which is row 1, column 0.
hints.approach: Binary search on the grid as if it were one flat sorted list of m·n numbers. Search positions 0 to m·n − 1. For the middle position, `divmod(mid, n)` gives its row and column: row mid // n, column mid % n. Compare that cell with the target and keep the half that can still hold it, exactly as in a plain binary search.
hints.whyNot: Checking every cell is O(m·n). Binary searching each row in turn is O(m log n), better but not O(log(m·n)). Searching the first column for the right row and then that row is also O(log m + log n) = O(log(m·n)); it works, but it's two searches where one will do.

slots.setup: `lo` = 0 and `hi` = m·n − 1: the first and last positions of the grid read row by row.
slots.loop: Keep going while `lo` ≤ `hi`; an empty range means the target isn't there.
slots.update: If the middle cell is smaller than the target, everything up to it is too, so `lo` = mid + 1; if it's larger, `hi` = mid − 1.
slots.record: Turn mid into a cell with `divmod(mid, n)` and compare `matrix[r][c]` with the target; equal means found.
slots.return: Return true as soon as the cell equals the target, and false once the range is empty.

solution.explanation: Each step halves the m·n positions still in play, so the loop runs about log₂(m·n) times: O(log(m·n)) time, the O(log n) choice on the Plan card with n the number of cells. Only a few integers are stored: O(1) space. `divmod(mid, n)` works because row r holds positions r·n to r·n + n − 1 of the flat list.

events.label: check
events.say: Positions {lo} to {hi} are left. The middle one, {mid}, is row {r}, column {c}: {row[c]}

events.label: found
events.say: {row[c]} is the target, so return true

events.label: go right
events.say: {row[c]} is smaller than {target}, and so is every position before it: search positions {mid + 1} to {hi}

events.label: go left
events.say: {row[c]} is bigger than {target}, and so is every position after it: search positions {lo} to {mid - 1}

events.label: not found
events.say: The range is empty, so {target} isn't in the grid: return false

predict.ask: Is the target after this cell?
Which row will the next middle position fall in?

related.relation: The same exact-match search on a sorted list; here each middle index is first turned into a row and a column.
